title: From entities to tables: normalization 1NF to BCNF by fixing a messy spreadsheet
summary: Normalization is "one fact, one place". Find the functional dependencies in the data, give each determinant a table keyed by it, and the keys and foreign keys you declare are those dependencies, enforced on every write.

examples.title: A test log spreadsheet as a table, and its three anomalies

annotations.note: No key and every column nullable: the shape of a spreadsheet. Its real key is (test_code, run_on), one run per test per day. A normalized table holds only columns that depend on its whole key, and here four columns don't.
REQ-1's title is stored in three rows and Mehmet's e-mail in two. Every repetition is a copy that can disagree with the others, and row 3 already does.

A functional dependency check: group by the determinant and count the distinct values that should depend on it. Run it against any import before you design the tables. Every row it returns is a contradiction a person has to resolve.
Without a key, nothing rejects a half-empty row. count(*) now says 5 and count(run_on) says 4, so every aggregate over the sheet has to know which rows aren't really runs.
REQ-2 lived only inside TC-3's run row. Deleting a run shouldn't delete a requirement, but in this shape it does, and nothing reports it.

examples.title: Decompose to 3NF: one table per determinant, then rebuild the sheet with joins

annotations.note: The title depended on the run only through req_code (a transitive dependency, which 3NF forbids). Now req_code is the key of a table that holds the title once. Codes as primary keys keep this example short; the keys lesson explains why a real schema adds a surrogate id and keeps UNIQUE (code).

test_code determines req_code, but test_code is only part of the run's key (test_code, run_on). Storing req_code per run was the 2NF violation. It now lives once per test case, and the foreign key is the link between the two tables.
tester determines the e-mail: the second 3NF fix. UNIQUE (email) also declares the reverse, one address per tester, which the spreadsheet couldn't express at all.
What's left needs the whole key: who ran this test on this day, and the result. The composite primary key is the sheet's implicit key, now enforced, and the CHECK closes the result vocabulary.
1NF: 'smoke, payment' was two values in one field. One row per tag can be matched exactly, counted and referenced. The anti-patterns lesson shows what the comma-separated version breaks.

Normalizing doesn't resolve contradictions, it exposes them. DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per req_code in ORDER BY order, the newest run's title. A plain SELECT DISTINCT req_code, req_title would produce two REQ-1 rows and fail on the primary key.
string_to_table (PG 14) splits on the comma, trim drops the space, and DISTINCT removes TC-1's tags, which the sheet repeated for each of its two runs.

Joining along the foreign keys gives the sheet's columns back: the decomposition is lossless, because each split was on a determinant that became the key of its new table. Every run now shows the one current title.
The dependency req_code -> req_title is now a primary key, so a second title is a duplicate key: SQLSTATE 23505.

examples.title: Beyond 3NF: a dependency whose determinant is not a key

annotations.note: Two candidate keys: (test_code, lab) and (test_code, tester). Every column belongs to one of them, and 3NF only restricts columns that belong to none, so this table is in 3NF.
BCNF's rule is stricter: every determinant must be a candidate key. tester determines lab but isn't a key here, so the fact is repeated per assignment, and the update anomaly is back.

testers is keyed by the determinant. UNIQUE (name, lab) follows from the primary key, but a foreign key must point at a unique constraint or index on exactly its columns; without it the FK below fails with SQLSTATE 42830.

The textbook BCNF split is assignments (test_code, tester), with no lab. That loses "one tester per test per lab", which then spans two tables and can't be a key. Keeping lab as a copy tied to testers by a composite foreign key keeps both rules declarable: deliberate, controlled redundancy, the subject of the next lesson.

ON UPDATE CASCADE carries the changed (name, lab) pair into every assignment, in the same statement. A move to 'ios' would fail with 23505 instead: TC-1 on iOS is Mehmet's, and the primary key still holds.
Zeynep works in android, so (Zeynep, ios) matches no tester row: SQLSTATE 23503. The copy can't drift from its source.

use_cases: Designing tables from a spreadsheet, a CSV export or a legacy table: list the dependencies first, then derive the tables
Cleaning an import: the GROUP BY ... HAVING count(DISTINCT ...) > 1 check lists every contradiction to resolve before loading
Reviewing a schema: a column that depends on part of a key, or on another non-key column, is an update anomaly waiting to happen
Deciding where a new column goes: next to the key that determines it
strengths: A rename or an e-mail change is a one-row UPDATE; in a flat table or a document store it is a multi-row update that a forgotten WHERE or a partial failure leaves inconsistent
The dependencies become PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE and REFERENCES declarations checked on every write, instead of invariants each Go or TS service has to remember
Things exist on their own: a requirement without tests or a tester without runs is a row, not a NULL-padded line
Narrow, keyed tables are what B-tree indexes, joins and the planner's per-column statistics are built for
weaknesses: Reads need joins: the spreadsheet comes back only by joining four tables, which reports and ORMs pay for on every read
BCNF can cost a rule: a dependency that ends up spanning two tables can't be a key and needs a composite foreign key, a trigger or application code
Normalization knows only the current value: a normalized title is today's title, so values that must be frozen (prices on invoices) need a deliberate copy
Over-splitting, such as a table per attribute, adds joins without removing any redundancy; stop where the dependencies stop

pitfalls.title: Loading with SELECT DISTINCT and trusting the result
pitfalls.detail: DISTINCT over (code, title) gives one row per distinct pair, so a contradiction becomes a duplicate key, or, with no key declared, a duplicate entity. Run the dependency check first and resolve what it finds.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO requirements SELECT DISTINCT req_code, req_title FROM sheet;
pitfalls.good: SELECT req_code FROM sheet GROUP BY req_code HAVING count(DISTINCT req_title) > 1;  -- resolve these, then load

pitfalls.title: Adding an id column and calling it normalized
pitfalls.detail: A surrogate key makes every row distinct, duplicates included, and leaves the dependencies among the other columns untouched. Every anomaly from example 1 survives it.
pitfalls.bad: ALTER TABLE sheet ADD COLUMN id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY;
pitfalls.good: requirements (code PRIMARY KEY, title), test_runs PRIMARY KEY (test_code, run_on), ...: the keys the dependencies imply

pitfalls.title: Normalizing away a snapshot
pitfalls.detail: The price on an order line or the title a test had when it ran may look like copies, but they are different facts: the value at that time. Replacing them with a join to the current value rewrites history.

pitfalls.title: Treating BCNF as the goal
pitfalls.detail: A decomposition that loses a business rule is worse than a controlled copy. Keep the copy and tie it to its source with a composite foreign key, as in example 3.

quiz.q: The sheet's key is (test_code, run_on), and req_code depends on test_code alone. Which normal form does that violate?
quiz.why: A non-key column that depends on part of a composite key is a partial dependency, which is exactly what 2NF forbids.

quiz.q: How do you check whether tester -> tester_email holds in imported data?
options: SELECT DISTINCT tester, tester_email FROM sheet
GROUP BY tester HAVING count(DISTINCT tester_email) > 1 returns no rows
quiz.why: The dependency holds when every tester has exactly one e-mail, so group by the determinant and look for more than one. UNIQUE (tester_email) checks the reverse direction.

quiz.q: lab_assignments in example 3 is in 3NF but not in BCNF. Why?
options: tester determines lab, and tester is not a candidate key
It has a composite primary key
quiz.why: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. 3NF lets this pass because lab is part of a candidate key, (test_code, lab).

quiz.q: Decomposing on a dependency X -> Y produces what?
options: A table keyed by X that holds Y, and X as a foreign key where Y used to be
A CHECK constraint relating X and Y
quiz.why: The determinant becomes a key, so each X maps to one Y by construction, and the original table keeps only the reference.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (primary keys, unique, foreign keys)

body:
## Concept

A table models one kind of thing, and every non-key column states a fact about that
thing. Normalization is the discipline that keeps it that way, phrased in terms of
**functional dependencies**: `X -> Y` holds when each value of `X` comes with exactly one
value of `Y` (a requirement code has one title; a tester has one e-mail address). `X` is
the **determinant**.

Data in which a determinant is not a key stores the same fact many times, and that
causes three **anomalies**:

- **Update**: a fact changed in one copy but not the others (REQ-1 has two titles).
- **Insertion**: a fact can't be recorded without an unrelated one (a requirement with
  no test run yet).
- **Deletion**: removing one fact removes another (the only run of TC-3 was the only
  record of REQ-2).

The cure is always the same move: give the determinant its own table, keyed by it, and
replace the copies with a foreign key. The normal forms name which dependencies are
left to remove.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Any OO language:** a class with `customerName` and `customerEmail` fields on every
  `Order` is the same smell as the spreadsheet; you would extract a `Customer` and hold
  a reference. Normalization is that refactoring, with a test (the dependency check)
  for when it's needed.
- **Java/JPA:** entities with `@ManyToOne` already produce normalized tables. The trap is
  the other direction: an `@Embedded` value object copied into many rows is
  denormalized, which is fine for a snapshot and a bug for shared data.
- **Document databases and JSON APIs:** a nested document per order is the
  spreadsheet again. It reads in one go, and every write to a shared value has to find
  all the copies.
- **Python/pandas:** `df.groupby('req_code')['req_title'].nunique() > 1` is the
  dependency check of example 1, and `drop_duplicates` is the `SELECT DISTINCT` you
  shouldn't trust blindly.

## How it works

The normal forms, as a checklist for each table (a candidate key is any minimal set of
columns that identifies a row):

1. **1NF**: every field holds one value; no lists in a cell, no `tag1, tag2, tag3`
   columns.
2. **2NF**: no non-key column depends on just part of a composite key (req_code on
   test_code alone).
3. **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column (req_title on req_code,
   tester_email on tester). The usual summary: every non-key column depends on the key,
   the whole key, and nothing but the key.
4. **BCNF**: every determinant is a candidate key, key columns included (tester -> lab
   in example 3).

The procedure that gets you there:

1. Name the entity each row is about and its real key.
2. List the dependencies; confirm them on real data with the `GROUP BY ... HAVING
   count(DISTINCT ...) > 1` check.
3. For each dependency whose determinant isn't a key, move the dependent columns to a
   table keyed by the determinant, and reference it.
4. Declare everything: the primary keys, UNIQUE constraints and foreign keys you end up
   with are the dependencies, and from then on the database rejects every write that
   would break one.

Splitting on a determinant that becomes a key is always lossless: joining back gives
exactly the original rows. Going from 3NF to BCNF, however, can lose a dependency, as in
example 3.

## Design notes

Aim for 3NF by default, check for BCNF, and treat every remaining copy as a decision you
can name. In practice the dependencies come from the domain, not from the data you
happen to have: four rows can't prove that a tester has one lab, only that no
counterexample exists yet. Ask whoever owns the rules.

Normalized does not mean "everything gets a surrogate id". Example 2 uses codes as keys
for brevity; a real TraceLite schema keys requirements by `id`, declares
`UNIQUE (project_id, code)`, and references the id, because codes get renamed. The
dependencies, and therefore the tables, are the same either way.

When a split would lose a rule, as in example 3, keep the redundant column and make the
database maintain it: a composite foreign key with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` turns a copy
into something that can't drift. The next lesson covers deliberate denormalization in
general, including the copies that aren't redundant at all, such as a price at the
time of sale.

files.examples/01_spreadsheet.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.modeling.normalization): one fact, one place; the keys say which place.
-- A test log kept in a spreadsheet, imported as-is: one row per test run.
CREATE TABLE sheet (
  test_code    text,
  run_on       date,
  req_code     text,
  req_title    text,
  tester       text,
  tester_email text,
  result       text,
  tags         text
);
INSERT INTO sheet VALUES
  ('TC-1', '2026-11-02', 'REQ-1', 'Pay by card',    'Ayşe',   'ayse@example.com',   'passed', 'smoke, payment'),
  ('TC-2', '2026-11-02', 'REQ-1', 'Pay by card',    'Mehmet', 'mehmet@example.com', 'failed', 'payment'),
  ('TC-1', '2026-11-09', 'REQ-1', 'Card payment',   'Ayşe',   'ayse@example.com',   'passed', 'smoke, payment'),
  ('TC-3', '2026-11-09', 'REQ-2', 'Invoice e-mail', 'Mehmet', 'mehmet@example.com', 'passed', 'email');

-- Update anomaly: REQ-1 was renamed in one row only. A dependency
-- req_code -> req_title holds when each code has exactly one title.
SELECT req_code, string_agg(DISTINCT req_title, ' | ' ORDER BY req_title) AS titles
FROM sheet
GROUP BY req_code
HAVING count(DISTINCT req_title) > 1;

-- Insertion anomaly: a requirement with no tests yet only fits as a
-- row of NULLs, and now "rows" no longer means "test runs".
INSERT INTO sheet (req_code, req_title) VALUES ('REQ-3', 'Refund to card');
SELECT count(*) AS rows, count(run_on) AS runs FROM sheet;

-- Deletion anomaly: TC-3's only run was logged by mistake. Deleting it
-- also deletes the only record that REQ-2 exists.
DELETE FROM sheet WHERE test_code = 'TC-3';
SELECT DISTINCT req_code, req_title FROM sheet ORDER BY req_code, req_title;
